At the height of the trade war between Trump and China, tariffs were being announced almost every week, prompting companies like Logitech to significantly raise the prices of their products in the United States.

Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that these tariffs were illegal and must be refunded to manufacturers. However, no company has yet been seen passing on the refunds to customers, and a class-action lawsuit is currently underway to try to correct this situation…

Trump Tariff Storm

Last year, Trump seized on the issue of the U.S. trade deficit with China and appeared to fantasise that by drastically raising tariffs on Chinese-made products, he could force companies like Apple to move their production lines back to the United States.

Of course, that was never going to happen. The U.S. lacks the manufacturing infrastructure, specialised expertise, and cheap labour required to produce consumer electronics at the scale demanded by the major brands.

Trump kept claiming that the tariffs would be borne by China, but in reality they were paid by the American brands importing the finished goods, and these additional costs were ultimately passed on to consumers through higher prices. At the peak of the storm, tariff rates reached as high as 145%.

Take Logitech as an example. The company raised the prices of roughly half of its product range by up to 25%.

Consumers Ought to Get a Refund

The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ruled that Trump had no authority to impose these tariffs unilaterally, and stated that the amounts paid by American businesses must be refunded. The refund process is currently underway.

The problem is that these costs were ultimately borne by consumers through price hikes, and none of the affected companies have shown any intention of refunding their customers so far.

The law firm CPM has filed a class-action lawsuit against Logitech over this, demanding refunds for consumers who paid higher prices during the period the tariffs were in effect.

9to5Mac Take

The principle behind the matter is indisputable. Companies paid the tariffs, passed the extra costs on to their customers, and are now receiving refunds from the government. Morally speaking, they ought to refund that portion of the purchase price to consumers who bought their products during this period.

However, putting it into practice is extremely challenging. Logitech would need to identify every transaction made through its vast network of third-party retailers, track what price consumers paid, and work out what proportion of that consisted of tariff costs.

If this lawsuit ultimately succeeds, it will undoubtedly set a very interesting precedent — though it has to be said that in class actions, the ones who really come out ahead are usually the lawyers, while the compensation actually received by consumers tends to be very small.
